references.text: The birth of Isaac and that Abraham gave him the name Isaac, which directly confirms the statement 'Abraham begot Isaac' in Gen 25:19.
God's promise to Abraham that Sarah will bear a son named Isaac, and that the covenant will be established with him - the direct background for the genealogy in 25:19.
The toledot formula of Ishmael ('this is the history of Ishmael') forms a direct parallel to the toledot formula of Isaac in 25:19.
One of the early toledot formulas in Genesis ('this is the book of the generations of Adam'), showing the literary structure that 25:19 is part of.
Paul quotes 'In Isaac shall your offspring be named' and highlights Isaac as the child of promise, not the child of the flesh - a theological elaboration of Isaac's special position as Abraham's son.
Both verses serve as introductions to genealogies and confirm the continuity of the promise through the line Abraham–Isaac.
Matthew confirms and reaffirms the same genealogical line as the foundation for the Messiah, illuminating the continuity of God's promise.
Acts links the same genealogical line directly to God's covenant and circumcision, enriching the understanding of the fulfillment of the promise.
Matthew 1:1 presents Jesus as the ultimate fulfillment of Abraham's promise, parallel to how Isaac was the first legitimate son.
Hebrews illuminates the theological significance of Isaac as the 'son of promise' and shows that his existence is central to faith.
The verse describes God's blessing as the prerequisite for Isaac's genealogy to continue, highlighting the continuity.
Luke confirms the same legitimate genealogical line (Abraham–Isaac–Jacob) as the foundation for Jesus' identity.
Romans explains the theological reason why Isaac is the legitimate heir, illuminating the significance of his place in the genealogy.
The verse describes the practical consequence of Isaac's role as heir, highlighting the significance of his place in the genealogy.
Galatians explains the theological reason why Isaac is the legitimate heir, illuminating the significance of his place in the genealogy.
